description: Team Pyrovex brings together curious minds passionate about AI/ML, data science, space, and real-world problem-solving. We turn NASA data into meaningful insights and engaging applications. We welcome teammates skilled in AI/ML, Python, data science, web development, GIS, UI/UX, research, or storytelling. Above all, we value curiosity, creativity, collaboration, and a willingness to learn. 🚀
summary:
India Burning Activity Calendar is a web app that turns 26 years of NASA FIRMS satellite fire detections into one consistent record of burning activity for any area of India.

What we built: We cleaned MODIS and VIIRS hotspots (Nov 2000 to Nov 2026), removed low-confidence and non-vegetation detections, and harmonized the sensors into MODIS-equivalent monthly counts. VIIRS is scaled to MODIS using the years when both flew, and early Terra-only months are corrected for Aqua’s late start. On held-out years the scaling had a median monthly error of about 12%. Users pick a region by preset, coordinates, or drawing on a map. The app then shows a year-by-month calendar in colorblind-safe colors, an anomaly view against the historical median, a seasonal cycle, a top-10 months table, and CSV download.

How it addresses the challenge: Hotspot counts no longer depend on which sensor made them, so patterns and anomalies stand out.

Why it matters: MODIS is nearing the end of its life. This approach keeps the long record usable, so emergency managers can see quickly whether the current month is unusual.
details:
What it does and how it works

PYROVEX built the India Burning Activity Calendar, a web app that turns 26 years of NASA FIRMS fire detections into one consistent record. We cleaned about 18 million MODIS and VIIRS hotspots over India (Nov 2000 to Nov 2026), removing low-confidence detections and non-vegetation sources such as industry and gas flares. We then harmonized the sensors into MODIS-equivalent monthly counts. VIIRS S-NPP is divided by its MODIS ratio, learned from the years both sensors flew. Early months with only Terra are scaled up with a calendar-month factor, because Aqua started in 2002. Users choose an area by preset, coordinates or drawing on a map, then see a year-by-month calendar, an anomaly view against the historical median, a seasonal cycle, a top-10 months table and a CSV download.

Benefits and intended impact

The sensor of origin no longer matters, so emergency managers, scientists and land managers can focus on patterns and anomalies, such as whether this month is unusually quiet or active. It keeps MODIS’s long history usable as VIIRS replaces it.

Tools

Python, DuckDB, pandas and Parquet for processing; Streamlit, Plotly, Folium, and Leaflet drawing tools for the app; GitHub and Streamlit Community Cloud for hosting. No special hardware.

Creativity

The calendar shows fire history at a glance. The viridis scale is colorblind-safe, and the anomaly view uses a diverging scale. Months with less certainty are marked with an asterisk.

Factors we considered

NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 see the same fires as S-NPP, so we used one VIIRS series to avoid double counting. MODIS and VIIRS report confidence differently, so each was filtered on its own scale. Held-out tests (2021 to 2026) gave a median monthly error of about 12%, with 90% of months within about ±34%, and no artificial steps in the annual totals. Limits: counts are hotspots, not burned area, scaling factors are national, and satellite overpass times drift.
